text.p: Wachovia Corp's $222 million agreement to buy 1st United Bancorp of Florida marks its third acquisition in two months and analysts say the deal won't be its last.
The bank holding company, which has dual headquarters in Winston-Salem N.C. and Atlanta, is currently the nation's 20th largest, with $48.5 billion in assets.

When it completes the three pending acquisitions - 1st United, Central Fidelity Banks Inc in Richmond, Va. and Jefferson Bankshares Inc in Charlottesville, Va.- it will become the 17th largest, with assets of more than $60 billion.

But rather than capture more states, analysts say Wachovia is likely to solidify its position with more acquisitions in its new territories of Florida and Virginia, where it faces formidible competition.

Having now moved into those areas with deals for the two banks there in June and July, Wachovia will most likely seek to build upon the beach-heads it has established after it has integrated the new acquisitions, analysts say.
"In Florida, they'll need to put a lot more meat on their bones to have a full-fledged franchise," said Kathryn Bissette, an analyst at Sterne Agee & Leach, in Atlanta.

Though the Boca Raton area is an upscale market, Wachovia will still have large and well-established competitors in the likes of First Union and NationsBank, out-of-state institutions which moved into Flordia years earlier. Wachovia will also butt heads with the same big regional banks in Virginia.
These three acquisitions are Wachovia's first in five years, during which it confined its operations to Georgia and the Carolinas.

"Some analysts were waiting for them to do something, but they were waiting to to do it the right way," said Maguerite Sons, an analyst at Interstate/Johnson Lane. "Wachovia has always been known as a conservative, quality institution."

But it appears now as if that wait is over. "Wachovia will continue to make selective acquisitions, mostly in markets that produce strong economic growth," said Ed Najarian, an analyst at Wheat First Butcher Singer.
He noted that the bank started a strategic review beginning in 1994 and that these acquisitions may be, in part, a result of that review.
The only thing that will slow the bank up, say analysts, is the price of neighboring institutions and the time it takes Wachovia to integrate the new banks into its system.
Sons said those integration issues, melding marketing and back office systems, could be completed as early as the first quarter of 1998.
And though banks, usually brought with shares of the acquiring institution, are not cheap at today's prices, Wachovia can afford to buy more.
"Prices are high, but they are selling at 2.6 times book value and 15 times estimated 1997 earnings," said Bissette. "They do have the currency to make premium deals."
Wachovia traded at 63-1/2 Thursday afternoon, off 1. 1st United traded at 20-1/4, up 1/2.
